extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and critics of tragedy; students and scholars of dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for composing and judging tragic (and related epic) poetry, covering subject/plot selection, character, recognition, diction, and staging. Emphasises unity of action, emotional effect (pity/fear), and appropriate stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection: few connected houses/families
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses, on the fortunes of Alcmaeon, Oedipus, Orestes, ... — a tragedy should be of this construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small number of connected families or a single, tightly related narrative sphere; select subjects whose histories contain moving incidents (e.g., kin-slaying, familial discovery). Avoid sprawling multiplicity of plots drawn from an entire epic (e.g., the whole Iliad) which overcomplicates a stage play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate (right) ending for tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy may end unhappily and this can be the 'right ending' if it follows the rules of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not condemn an unhappy ending simply for being unhappy; judge ending by its fit within the plot's construction and its tragic effectiveness on stage and in competition (example: many of Euripides' plays end unhappily but may be most tragic in effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear through plot structure, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way, and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that even a listener (without visual spectacle) will feel horror and pity (e.g., Oedipus). Avoid relying on spectacle that produces only a sense of the monstrous rather than the properly tragic; spectacle is a lesser, extraneous method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that arouse pity/fear: relations between persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity/fear must happen between persons who are either friends or enemies or indifferent — greatest effect when between those near or dear (kin or close relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer incidents where familial or close relationships are involved (brother kills brother, son his father, mother her son, etc.). If actions occur between strangers or enemies there is less ground for pity unless the suffering itself is pitiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of the horrific deed and their ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic deed may be done consciously with knowledge, done in ignorance with discovery afterwards, or be about to be done then discovered; these are the only possible ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking: (best) deed perpetrated in ignorance with discovery afterwards (startling effect without gratuitous shock); (next) deed perpetrated knowingly; (least artistic) being about to act and then not acting (shocking without tragic consequence). Examples: Oedipus (ignorance discovered later), Medea (witting murder), Antigone/Haemon (threats that do not culminate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness with traditional material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may not destroy the framework of received legends but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect traditional facts when using legendary material, but introduce original handling, episodes, or devices that heighten tragic effect while preserving core elements (do not merely recount legend mechanically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: moral goodness (purpose) as primary aim
rubrics_metrics.description: First, and most important, character must be good: any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be expressive of character; the character will be good if the purpose is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to class (a woman or a slave can be 'good' in their class). Ensure moral purpose is evident through actions and speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (fitness to role/class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the character must exhibit propriety: qualities should be appropriate to the person's sex, status, and role (e.g., manly valour suits men, not women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incongruous traits (e.g., valour in a woman when inappropriate) that violate audience expectations of propriety and spoil credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: true to life (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The character must be true to life — distinct from goodness and propriety — i.e., believable within human behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray types faithfully even as you ennoble them; characters should act in ways consistent with real human motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be consistent: even if the person being imitated is inconsistent, the portrayal must be 'consistently inconsistent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless degradations or abrupt, unexplained changes (examples of faults: Menelaus in Orestes, Iphigenia's inconsistent portrayals). Every trait should cohere with the established character pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and character should follow necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: As in plot structure, portraiture of character should aim at the necessary or the probable; a person of given character should speak or act in a given way by necessity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure causes and consequences follow plausibly from established character and prior incidents; do not introduce irrational acts within the action itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Deus ex Machina' within action
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Deus ex Machina' must not bring about the unraveling within the action proper — it should be employed only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve central plot complications by arbitrary divine intervention or implausible external forces; if irrational elements exist they should lie outside the immediate tragic action (example: misuse in Medea or Return of the Greeks in the Iliad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis): prefer natural incident-driven discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions vary (by signs/tokens, poet-invented speech, memory, reasoning), but of all recognitions the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves — startling discovery made by natural means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of artistic merit: (best) recognition arising naturally from the plot (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia), (next) recognition by reasoning, (weaker) recognition by memory/association, (weak/less artistic) recognition by external tokens, and (poor) recognitions invented by the poet that the plot does not require (e.g., a character suddenly saying 'I am X' for no plot reason). Avoid artifices like arbitrary tokens or verbal self-revelation that feel imposed by the poet rather than the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of recognition (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions include: (1) by signs (congenital or acquired tokens, scars, necklaces), (2) poet-invented verbal revelations, (3) memory/association (sight or sound evokes recollection), (4) by process of reasoning, and (5) composite/false inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the varieties and choose forms that best suit the plot's plausibility; tokens and formal proofs are less artistic than recognitions produced by turning-points in the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualisation and stage-awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes; seeing everything vividly as if a spectator, to discover what is fitting and avoid inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with situational awareness to catch stage oversights (example: failure in Carcinus where a character's departure was overlooked). Consider gestures and physical expression appropriate to the emotions (agitated storms, angry rages) to increase conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot planning: sketch general outline, then amplify with relevant episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should first sketch the general outline of the story and then fill in episodes and amplify in detail; episodes must be relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clear beginning, middle, and end; keep episodes short in drama (they extend Epic); ensure each episode contributes to the unity of action (example: Odyssey's episodic material vs. concentrated dramatic action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural division: Complication and Unravelling (Denouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts — Complication (from action's start to the turning-point) and Unravelling (from the change to the end). Identity of a tragedy is judged by sameness of both Complication and Unravelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master both knot-tying (complication) and unravelling; many poets tie well but fail to unravel properly. Use Reversal (peripeteia) and Recognition as chief mechanisms in complex plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of tragedy (complex, pathetic, ethical, simple)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds: Complex (depends on Reversal and Recognition), Pathetic (motive is passion), Ethical (motive is ethical), and Simple (no recognition or reversal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim, if possible, to combine the greatest number of poetic elements (reversal, recognition, scenes of suffering) to achieve the most complete tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action: avoid epic multiplicity in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy — avoid multiplicity of plots; tragedy should have a single action whole and complete with a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a portion of a larger story rather than dramatizing an entire epic; poets who dramatise the whole Fall of Troy or whole Niobe fail or have poor success. Epic allows multiplicity and episodes; tragedy demands unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and share in the action; it should be an integral part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that act merely as interludes unrelated to the piece (a practice attributed to later poets/Agathon). The Chorus ought to participate meaningfully in the dramatic action, as in Sophocles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (conceptual content) and speech effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes every effect to be produced by speech: proof and refutation; excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger); suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic incidents must be treated toward these aims; incidents should often speak for themselves while speeches should produce intended effects through the speaker. Thought as treated in Rhetoric is central to dramatic persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Modes of Utterance (delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction includes modes of utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question, answer, etc.), but proper delivery belongs to the art of Delivery rather than to poetry alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should be aware of these modes but not be censured for fine-grained issues of utterance that belong to performers or masters of delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean; balance of current and rare words
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean: use current/proper words for clarity, and unusual (strange/rare/metaphorical/lengthened/altered) words for loftiness — but in moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judicious mixture raises diction above the commonplace: too many ordinary words make it mean; too many rare/metaphorical words make it a riddle or jargon. Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words used sparingly add distinction without obscurity. Command of metaphor is crucial and marks genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate lexical choices by genre/metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different word-types suit different genres: compound words for dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic; heroic metre admits rare words and metaphors, iambic should resemble familiar speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction consistent with metre and genre (heroic metre fits grand diction; iambic expects language similar to prose). Do not mix metres or incompatible diction; metre selection follows nature and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poetry requirements: unity-of-scope, scale and heroic metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic, like tragedy, must have a single action whole and complete; it differs in scale (can enlarge), and uses heroic metre which admits rare words and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep epic subjects within a beginning and end that can be viewed as a whole; exploit narrative form to present simultaneous lines of action and relevant episodes for grandeur, but avoid incoherent multiplicity that defeats unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's presence: speak little in own person
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; Homer is praised for bringing in characters rather than the poet appearing throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimise authorial intrusions; let characters and actions carry the imitation rather than frequent direct address by the poet-narrator.
